power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: M-SEC: A Clinical Listening Framework for Menopause-Informed Mental Health Care

text.text: Clinicians in mental health settings are frequently the first professionals to encounter patients navigating the menopausal transition, yet most receive little to no training in how hormonal change presents in our offices, or even that it presents there at all.

As a result, symptoms rooted in perimenopause and menopause, including disrupted sleep, mood instability, and cognitive difficulty, are often unrecognized as hormonal and misattributed to primary psychiatric conditions, leaving patients misunderstood and undertreated.
This paper introduces M-SEC, a clinical framework that organizes attention around three converging domains: Sleep Disruption, Emotion Regulation, and Cognitive Changes.
We argue that these domains represent the signal most visible to mental health clinicians and most likely to be missed as hormonal in origin.

We present the conceptual rationale for M-SEC, situate it alongside existing models of midlife mental health care, and outline its application toward more accurate recognition and collaborative, medically informed care.
M-SEC is offered as a foundation for menopauseinformed clinical practice and as a shared language for a field that currently lacks one.
The menopausal transition is a near-universal experience, affecting essentially half the population and unfolding across a decade or more from perimenopause through the postmenopausal years.
At any given moment, a substantial proportion of adult patients in mental health settings are somewhere within this window.
Despite this scale, the clinical workforce remains strikingly unprepared to recognize and respond to its psychological presentations.
The evidence for this training gap is now well documented, at least among physicians.

In a cross-sectional survey of family medicine, internal medicine, and obstetrics and gynecology residents, only 6.8 percent felt adequately prepared to manage patients experiencing menopause, and roughly one in five reported receiving no menopause-related instruction whatsoever during residency (Kling et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In a cross-sectional survey of family medicine, internal medicine, and obstetrics and gynecology residents, only 6.8 percent felt adequately prepared to manage patients experiencing menopause, and roughly one in five reported receiving no menopause-related instruction whatsoever during residency <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Kling et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Subsequent work has reinforced this picture: in a national survey of obstetrics and gynecology residency program directors, only about a third reported that their program included a dedicated menopause curriculum, even as the overwhelming majority agreed such training was needed (Allen et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Subsequent work has reinforced this picture: in a national survey of obstetrics and gynecology residency program directors, only about a third reported that their program included a dedicated menopause curriculum, even as the overwhelming majority agreed such training was needed <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allen et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Earlier needs assessments reached similar conclusions (Christianson et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Earlier needs assessments reached similar conclusions <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Christianson et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, this literature concentrates almost entirely on medical specialties whose scope of practice explicitly includes the menopausal transition.

Mental health clinicians, psychologists, social workers, professional counselors, and marriage and family therapists, who typically receive far less training in reproductive physiology than physicians do, are largely absent from this body of research.
The near-silence is itself telling.
If the specialists whose training most directly covers the transition still report this degree of unpreparedness, mental health clinicians are unlikely to be any better positioned.
They encounter these patients constantly, but through a psychological rather than a physiological lens.
The problem, moreover, runs deeper than general unfamiliarity with the transition.
Where training addresses menopause at all, it tends to frame it as a physiological event, defined by hot flashes, night sweats, and menstrual change.

What is largely absent, and absent in mental health training especially, is the recognition that much of the menopausal transition's symptom burden is experienced not physically but psychologically: disrupted sleep, mood instability, and cognitive difficulty.
The gap is therefore twofold.
The first is a gap in awareness: many mental health clinicians do not recognize the menopausal transition as falling within their purview at all, and so it never enters their clinical thinking.
The second is a gap in interpretation: even when these symptoms are noticed, they are read as a primary psychiatric condition rather than a hormonal one.
In effect, many mental health clinicians may share the assumption common in the wider culture: that menopause is essentially a matter of hot flashes and night sweats.
Under that assumption, psychological symptoms are not recognized as part of the transition, even when classic physical signs appear alongside them.
When these presentations are not recognized as hormonally influenced, they are readily assigned to primary psychiatric diagnoses.
Survey data are consistent with this pattern.

Among women who reported feeling misdiagnosed during the transition, the treatments they had received clustered heavily in the mental health domain, with roughly one in three treated for anxiety, one in four for depression, a comparable share for mood disturbance, and a smaller proportion for panic (industry-sponsored survey; Biote, 2025).
text.formatted: Among women who reported feeling misdiagnosed during the transition, the treatments they had received clustered heavily in the mental health domain, with roughly one in three treated for anxiety, one in four for depression, a comparable share for mood disturbance, and a smaller proportion for panic (industry-sponsored survey; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Biote, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The conditions to which the menopause transition is misattributed are, overwhelmingly, mental health diagnoses.
Beyond the training gap itself lies a deeper structural absence.

No agreed-upon framework exists to help a mental health clinician know what to listen for in the menopausal transition, how to distinguish a hormonally driven presentation from a primary psychiatric one, or when to coordinate with medical colleagues.
In its absence, clinicians are left to improvise, and recognition rests on the awareness of the individual practitioner rather than any common standard.

Such a standard matters not only for the individual clinician, who gains a dependable way to recognize what is otherwise easily missed, but for the field, which gains a shared language for these presentations across providers.
It is this absence that the present framework seeks to address.
The menopausal transition's tendency to present through psychological symptoms places mental health clinicians in a uniquely consequential role.
Whether a patient self-refers or arrives already carrying a psychiatric label, mental health clinicians gather clinical information at a depth found nowhere else in the care pathway.

The standard mental health intake, a detailed symptom review, structured assessment instruments, and an in-depth clinical interview, produces a far more granular picture of sleep, mood, and cognition than the brief encounters typical of primary or gynecologic care, where a diagnosis such as anxiety may be reached on comparatively limited data.
This depth of assessment is precisely the substrate required to distinguish a hormonally driven presentation from a primary psychiatric one.
What has been missing is not the clinical information, nor the clinical skill to gather it, but an interpretive framework that directs this existing rigor toward the hormonal transition.
It is this framework that M-SEC provides.
M-SEC is designed to draw on information already gathered as part of a standard clinical assessment.
M-SEC is a clinical lens: a way of interpreting information already in hand.

The mental health clinician conducting a thorough intake already has every relevant piece of information; M-SEC provides the means to connect them, so that a hormonal influence is considered when the pattern warrants it.

As such, M-SEC is a clinical listening heuristic designed to help mental health clinicians recognize the possible hormonal basis of presentations based on information they are already hearing from their clients.

The acronym directs attention to three converging domains, Sleep Disruption, Emotion Regulation, and Cognitive Changes, chosen because they represent the signals most visible within a mental health assessment and, simultaneously, among the signals most likely to be produced by the menopausal transition yet misread as primary psychiatric conditions (Baker et al., 2018; Cohen et al., 2006; Freeman et al., 2006; Gurvich et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The acronym directs attention to three converging domains, Sleep Disruption, Emotion Regulation, and Cognitive Changes, chosen because they represent the signals most visible within a mental health assessment and, simultaneously, among the signals most likely to be produced by the menopausal transition yet misread as primary psychiatric conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baker et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cohen et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Freeman et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Gurvich et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these three domains is at once a routine focus of mental health assessment and a documented domain of possible change during the menopausal transition.

First, sleep disruption is often the first domain to shift, and it is among the most common features of the transition, with prevalence rising from the reproductive years into perimenopause and postmenopause, where estimates commonly fall between forty and sixty percent (Baker et al., 2018).
text.formatted: First, sleep disruption is often the first domain to shift, and it is among the most common features of the transition, with prevalence rising from the reproductive years into perimenopause and postmenopause, where estimates commonly fall between forty and sixty percent <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baker et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Second, emotion regulation is commonly affected, though the association is more nuanced than it is often portrayed.

The transition is not a universal trigger for mood disorder, and a recent synthesis of prospective studies cautions against assuming that it uniformly raises the risk of depression or anxiety (Brown et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The transition is not a universal trigger for mood disorder, and a recent synthesis of prospective studies cautions against assuming that it uniformly raises the risk of depression or anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brown et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: What the evidence does support is that the transition is a window of heightened vulnerability for identifiable subgroups, particularly women with a prior history of depression, severe vasomotor symptoms, or recent stressful life events, with some prospective work finding elevated risk of new-onset depressive symptoms during perimenopause itself (Cohen et al., 2006; Freeman et al., 2006).
text.formatted: What the evidence does support is that the transition is a window of heightened vulnerability for identifiable subgroups, particularly women with a prior history of depression, severe vasomotor symptoms, or recent stressful life events, with some prospective work finding elevated risk of new-onset depressive symptoms during perimenopause itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cohen et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Freeman et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The presentation in this window is also frequently characterized by anxiety and irritability rather than classic low mood; these symptoms are highly prevalent, may precede depressive symptoms, and have historically received less attention than depression (Bromberger et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The presentation in this window is also frequently characterized by anxiety and irritability rather than classic low mood; these symptoms are highly prevalent, may precede depressive symptoms, and have historically received less attention than depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bromberger et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Third, cognitive changes are frequently reported: many women describe experiences such as brain fog, word-finding difficulty, and forgetfulness during the transition, with roughly two-thirds reporting concerns of this kind (Gurvich et al., 2026; Greendale et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Third, cognitive changes are frequently reported: many women describe experiences such as brain fog, word-finding difficulty, and forgetfulness during the transition, with roughly two-thirds reporting concerns of this kind <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Gurvich et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Greendale et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Because these experiences overlap with the presentations of several mental health conditions and are easily attributed to stress, they are readily dismissed or misassigned, folded into an attentional or trauma-related explanation when they may instead reflect the hormonal transition, particularly when they emerge alongside changes in sleep and emotion regulation.
In practice, M-SEC functions less as a protocol than as a listening posture.

It asks the clinician, when a patient in the midlife window presents with difficulties in sleep, emotion regulation, or cognition, to hold the hormonal transition as an active hypothesis rather than a diagnosis of last resort.
As noted, the domains it names are already central to any thorough mental health assessment; what it changes is interpretation.

A pattern that might otherwise read as a treatment-resistant depression, or a late-emerging attentional problem, or generalized anxiety, is instead examined for its timing, its convergence, and its relationship to the reproductive stage.
Recognition, in this frame, is not the endpoint; it is what makes appropriate care possible.

The menopausal transition has an established evidence base for treatment, spanning hormonal and non-hormonal options (Maki et al., 2018), and a patient whose symptoms are never recognized as hormonal cannot be connected to it.
text.formatted: The menopausal transition has an established evidence base for treatment, spanning hormonal and non-hormonal options <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Maki et al., 2018)</ref>, and a patient whose symptoms are never recognized as hormonal cannot be connected to it.

text.text: Where the pattern suggests a hormonal contribution, M-SEC orients the clinician toward collaborative, medically informed care, situating the mental health provider as one node in a broader network rather than the sole author of the treatment plan.

The aim is not for mental health clinicians to manage the transition themselves, but to recognize its signature early and to route the patient toward the medical evaluation, and the evidence-based treatment, that recognition warrants.
Several limitations warrant note.

Most fundamentally, M-SEC is a conceptual framework rather than a validated instrument; its domains and their convergence are grounded in existing literature, but the heuristic itself awaits empirical testing.

It also rests on an evidence base that is still developing and at times inconsistent, most notably regarding the strength and direction of the association between the transition and mood, which counsels against treating any single domain as diagnostic in isolation.

Finally, M-SEC is deliberately bounded to the task of recognition; the differential-diagnostic reasoning and treatment decisions that follow lie beyond its scope and depend on the clinician's broader training and judgment.
M-SEC does not enter an empty field.

Considerable work has characterized the physiology of the menopausal transition, its symptom burden, and its associations with mood, sleep, and cognition, and clinical guidance exists for its medical management.

The closest existing framework is the set of guidelines for the evaluation and treatment of perimenopausal depression issued by The North American Menopause Society and the National Network of Depression Centers, which direct clinicians to identify the menopausal stage, assess overlapping menopausal and psychiatric symptoms, and use structured scales to disentangle them (Maki et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The closest existing framework is the set of guidelines for the evaluation and treatment of perimenopausal depression issued by The North American Menopause Society and the National Network of Depression Centers, which direct clinicians to identify the menopausal stage, assess overlapping menopausal and psychiatric symptoms, and use structured scales to disentangle them <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Maki et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: M-SEC is consistent with that guidance but differs in two respects.
The first concerns scope.
Guidance of this kind centers on depression, yet depression is frequently not the presentation a mental health clinician actually hears in this window.

Anxiety and irritability are among the most prevalent psychological features of the transition; long-running cohort research operationalizes perimenopausal anxiety as a symptom cluster built around irritability and nervousness, and notes that anxiety is highly prevalent, may precede depressive symptoms, and has received far less attention than depression (Bromberger et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Anxiety and irritability are among the most prevalent psychological features of the transition; long-running cohort research operationalizes perimenopausal anxiety as a symptom cluster built around irritability and nervousness, and notes that anxiety is highly prevalent, may precede depressive symptoms, and has received far less attention than depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bromberger et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: A depression-centered frame therefore risks missing what is often the most prominent signal.

M-SEC does not confine itself to a single diagnosis; it organizes attention across the convergence of sleep, emotion regulation, and cognition, where emotion regulation is understood to encompass the anxiety and irritability that so often dominate the midlife presentation.

The second difference concerns audience: M-SEC is addressed specifically to mental health clinicians as the professionals often best positioned to recognize the pattern, rather than to the gynecologic and primary care settings where such guidance is more commonly applied.
Others have named the underlying problem.

Recent commentary observes that primary care and psychiatry tend to operate through divergent disciplinary lenses, so that the same midlife symptoms are read as hormonal in one setting and psychiatric in another, with misattribution and fragmented care the result (Bachkangi, 2026).
text.formatted: Recent commentary observes that primary care and psychiatry tend to operate through divergent disciplinary lenses, so that the same midlife symptoms are read as hormonal in one setting and psychiatric in another, with misattribution and fragmented care the result <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bachkangi, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: M-SEC takes the next step, converting that account of the problem into an operational heuristic a clinician can apply in the room.

Where existing models tend to address the transition either as a physiological process oriented toward medical treatment, or as a matter of psychological adjustment oriented toward coping and support, M-SEC occupies the space between: it is neither a treatment protocol nor a coping model, but a recognition heuristic, aimed at the moment of interpretation that precedes and enables appropriate care.

In this sense it complements rather than competes with existing frameworks, supplying the connective step that routes a patient from a mental health setting toward the medical evaluation the evidence supports.
M-SEC is introduced here as a conceptual framework, and its presentation as such carries a clear implication for what follows.

The heuristic invites empirical evaluation: studies of whether training in M-SEC improves clinicians' recognition of hormonally influenced presentations, whether it shortens the path to appropriate referral, and whether it changes patient outcomes.
Recognition is the necessary first step, but it raises a further question: once a clinician's attention has been oriented, how is that awareness carried forward in a consistent way?

This points beyond the present framework, toward structured approaches that support the next stage of the work, the organization of what recognition surfaces and its communication to medical colleagues.
Such approaches build upon the listening posture described here rather than adding to it, and their development is a direction for future work.

The present paper does not offer that validation; it offers the framework on which such work can be built, and a shared vocabulary through which a field that has lacked one can begin to organize its attention.
This paper presents a conceptual clinical framework developed independently by the authors through the Midlife Training Institute.
No human participants were recruited and no participant data were collected or analyzed, so institutional review board oversight did not apply.
